Terminate

TUR-mih-nayt — contains 'terminal,' the end point; to terminate is to reach the terminal. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To terminate to bring something to an end or conclusion.

The airline had to terminate the flight early and land at the nearest airport due to a mechanical issue.

Worked Example

A gym member keeps missing payments for six months despite several warning emails. Eventually, the gym's manager cancels the membership entirely and revokes the member's access to the building.

Officially ending something completely, with no continuation, is to terminate it. Unlike 'pause,' which is temporary, terminate means bringing something to a full and final end.

Antonyms

How Strong Is It? — pause → abolish → terminate

pause vs. terminate

pause vs. terminate: Pause is weaker than terminate — pausing something stops it only temporarily, while terminate means ending it completely and for good.

abolish vs. terminate

abolish vs. terminate: Abolish can be stronger than terminate: terminate usually ends a single agreement or process, but abolish wipes out an entire system, law, or practice altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — -termin-

root — -termin-: end, boundary (Latin)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin terminare comes from terminus, meaning 'end, boundary.' To terminate something is to bring it to its boundary line and stop it there for good.
